newsitem.title: UK: Catholic killed in N.Ireland sectarian attack.
newsitem.headline: Catholic killed in N.Ireland sectarian attack.

text.p: The body of a 62-year-old Roman Catholic was found on a Northern Ireland country road on Tuesday after what police said was a sectarian murder.

He had been abducted from a club of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), an Irish nationalist and Catholic sports group, on Monday night and was shot after a struggle, police at Randalstown, scene of the crime, said.
It was thought to be the third sectarian killing this year after the shooting of a Catholic father of nine in Belfast in April and the beating to death of a Catholic in Portadown earlier this month.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the killing but Protestant Loyalists were under suspicion.
The killing took place amid fears that Loyalist extremists, who want the province to remain British, have abandoned a ceasefire they declared in October 1994.
In Dublin, the leader of Ireland's Protestants told his church's annual synod that he feared sectarian tension bubbling under Northern Ireland's tense political climate could erupt.
"If sectarianism continues at its present level, the whole of our society will be plunged into a new nightmare of suffering and uncertainty," Archbishop Robin Eames said.
He wondered aloud whether new laws might be needed to outlaw sectarianism after a spate of church-burning in Northern Ireland and tit-for-tat attacks by extremists.
"Are changes in the law desirable to give greater assistance to this process? Is the current law really geared to outlaw sectarianism?" he asked.

Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, have been blamed for a series of attacks on Catholic or Irish nationalist targets in recent months since their Irish Republican Army (IRA) foes ended their own truce in 1996.

The IRA, a Catholic-backed guerrilla organisation which is fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, is demanding that its political wing, Sinn Fein, gain a place at Northern Ireland peace talks without preconditions.
Tuesday's victim was described by police superintendent Robin Campbell as an "upstanding member of the community" whose death bore "all the hallmarks of a sectarian murder."

The murder took place as representatives of the Loyalists' political wings were due to hold talks with Majorie Mowlam, Northern Ireland Secretary in the Labour government which won elections on May 1.
Sinn Fein, which saw its top two leaders win British parliamentary seats on May 1, is excluded from the talks because of the IRA's ending of its ceasefire.
Tension has been high in recent months with the IRA targeting British security force members and Loyalists launching a spate of apparently retaliatory attacks.
